title: Damascus Document — Hobah Translation
about: The Damascus Document is a Jewish sectarian work known from medieval Cairo Geniza copies (CD) and multiple ancient Qumran fragments. It combines an admonition about Israel's history and the community's origins with legal rules for covenant members living in camps and settlements. No single ancient manuscript preserves the whole work.

translation.status: Hobah provisional source-language reading translation of major preserved Damascus Document passages
translation.base_text: The Hebrew Damascus Document tradition represented by CD A/B and the Qumran fragments, keeping the Cairo and Qumran witnesses conceptually distinct
translation.method: Fresh modern-English rendering from the Hebrew sense of substantially preserved passages. Because the work survives in overlapping witnesses with gaps and different arrangements, this reader does not pretend to reconstruct a single perfect archetype. Brackets indicate damaged or uncertain sense.
translation.confidence: Medium-high in continuous CD passages; medium or lower where Qumran fragments supply broken or variant material
translation.notes: This edition presents the major admonition and legal themes in source order where possible. It is a reading translation, not a diplomatic edition or a silent conflation of every fragment.
translation.license_note: The ancient Hebrew witnesses are public domain. Hobah English wording is newly prepared for this project.

chapters.label: Admonition I — A remnant awakened
chapters.text: Listen, all who know righteousness and understand the works of God. He has a dispute with all flesh and will bring judgment upon those who reject him. When Israel was unfaithful and abandoned the covenant, he hid his face from them and gave them into the sword. Yet he remembered the covenant of the ancestors and left a remnant. After a period of wrath he visited them and caused a root of planting to spring from Israel and Aaron, so that his land might again be possessed and the goodness of his soil enjoyed.

chapters.label: Admonition II — The Teacher and the covenant
chapters.text: For years the remnant walked like blind people searching for the way. Then God considered their deeds and raised for them a Teacher of Righteousness to guide them in the path of his heart and to make known what he would do in the last generation. Those who entered the new covenant were required to turn from stubbornness, to seek the law, and to listen to the interpretation given within the community. Those who despised correction and chose smooth words were counted with the faithless.

chapters.label: Admonition III — The three nets of Belial
chapters.text: Belial sets traps before Israel, and three are especially named: sexual immorality, riches, and profanation of the sanctuary. By these he catches people who believe they are righteous while they twist the law for desire or gain. The covenant members are warned not to multiply wives contrary to the pattern of creation, not to take forbidden unions, not to steal through deceitful commerce, and not to bring impurity into what is holy.

chapters.label: Admonition IV — Covenant history and judgment
chapters.text: The document looks back to the Watchers, their sons, the generation of the flood, and later rebels as examples of those who followed the stubborn inclination of the heart. Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are praised for keeping the commands made known to them. The lesson is repeated: God remembers covenant loyalty across generations, but persistent rebellion reaches an appointed judgment. A person's claim to belong to Israel does not protect deliberate lawlessness.

chapters.label: Admonition V — The faithful remnant
chapters.text: Those who hold fast to God's commands in the time of wickedness are described as the people who know his name. They are to love each person according to his standing, hate the works of corruption, separate from the men of the pit, and wait for God's visitation. The covenant is not merely a private belief; it orders speech, money, family life, worship, discipline, and the treatment of one's neighbour.

chapters.label: Rule I — Sabbath
chapters.text: On the Sabbath no one shall pursue ordinary work or arrange business for profit. Speech about buying and selling is restricted, and burdens are not to be carried as on a common day. A person shall not travel beyond the limit fixed by the rule for ordinary purposes. Food and drink are prepared with regard for the holiness of the day. The law also discusses rescue of human and animal life, showing the community's attempt to define how rest and mercy meet in practical cases.

chapters.label: Rule II — Purity and food
chapters.text: A person who is unclean shall not enter sacred food or the assembly's holy portions until the required purification and time are complete. The rule distinguishes clean and unclean foods and warns against consuming what has been improperly prepared. Water used for purification must itself meet the rule's conditions. Bodily discharge, contact with impurity, and the handling of sacred things are treated as matters of covenant discipline rather than private preference.

chapters.label: Rule III — Marriage and household
chapters.text: Marriage is governed by the law of permitted kinship and covenant faithfulness. A man shall not take a woman forbidden by close relation, and sexual conduct that violates the Torah is condemned. Parents are responsible for teaching children, and the household is expected to live under the same covenant standards as the wider camp. The document treats family order as part of holiness, not as an area outside the law.

chapters.label: Rule IV — Vows, oaths, and truthful speech
chapters.text: No one shall swear carelessly by the divine Name. Vows and oaths are regulated so that sacred speech is not used to strengthen deception. An overseer may examine certain commitments, and a person must not use a vow to make evil lawful. Truthful testimony is required, while slander, false accusation, and malicious speech bring discipline.

chapters.label: Rule V — Property, trade, and neighbours
chapters.text: The covenant member shall not defraud a companion, conceal dishonest gain, or use another person's need for exploitation. Dealings with outsiders are also regulated so that the community does not participate in idolatrous commerce or unlawful profit. Lost property, deposits, debts, and shared resources are treated as moral matters. Wealth is one of Belial's traps when it becomes stronger than covenant loyalty.

chapters.label: Rule VI — Judges, overseers, and camps
chapters.text: Judges shall be trustworthy, knowledgeable in the law, and able to examine a matter without favour. Each camp has an overseer who knows the members, instructs the ignorant, receives those seeking admission, and guards the common order. He must not rule by anger or greed. The members are ranked and examined, yet authority itself remains accountable to the covenant.

chapters.label: Rule VII — Admission, discipline, and restoration
chapters.text: A person entering the covenant is examined concerning conduct and understanding. Deliberate lying, sexual wrongdoing, contempt for the rule, slander, theft, and repeated rebellion bring penalties proportionate to the offence. Some acts require temporary exclusion; persistent defiance can end membership. Correction is meant to preserve a holy community, and restoration is possible where the rule allows genuine return.

chapters.label: Closing admonition — Waiting for visitation
chapters.text: Those who walk in these statutes during the age of wickedness are called to remain faithful until God's visitation. The document expects a future resolution in which deceit is exposed, the wicked receive their reward, and those who held to the covenant are remembered for good. Its closing voice is therefore both legal and apocalyptic: keep the rule now because history is moving toward judgment.
